items.one_idea: Longest Consecutive Sequence: put all numbers in a hash set and start counting only from numbers whose x-1 is not in the set, so every number is walked at most once and no sorting is needed.
items.visual_idea: A number line with the array values as filled cells and gaps empty; cells with a filled left neighbour are greyed out, cells with an empty left neighbour get a start flag and a pointer slides right counting while the next cell is filled, with the run length shown. Actual Python code visible in readable chunks synced to the voice.
items.example: EXAMPLE nums = [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]: run starts 1, 100, 200; run from 1 is 1,2,3,4 so the answer is 4. [0,3,7,2,5,8,4,6,0,1] gives 9. Without the skip check on [1..2000] there are 2,001,000 set lookups vs 4,000 with it (EXAMPLE).
facts_to_verify: Problem paraphrased from doocs mirror of LeetCode 128. Hash set average O(1) lookup per Wikipedia/Python FAQ. O(n) time and O(n) extra space is our own derived analysis. Code was run: 4, 9, 0 (qa/d017/run_output.txt). 2 million vs 4 thousand lookups is EXAMPLE arithmetic on [1..2000].

items.title: Subarray Sum Equals K: prefix sum aur hash map se count
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: कितने subarrays का sum exactly k है, negatives के साथ?
items.hook_source: Interviewer asked: the problem as one complete question; interviewer_asked is the unused hook type of the last six built (d012-d017). No company claim.
items.hook_10s: Interviewer ने पूछा: कितने subarrays का sum exactly k है, negatives के साथ? Subarray यानी array का continuous हिस्सा. [Frame 0: array 3, 4, -3, 2, 1, 1 with a bracket on 4, -3, 2 and the label sum = 3]
items.one_idea: Subarray Sum Equals K: a subarray ending at the current index sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix sum equals current_prefix - k, so keep a hash map of prefix-sum counts and add seen[current - k] at each step; sliding window fails because negatives break monotonic growth.
items.visual_idea: The array as a row of cells with a running prefix-sum strip underneath; at each cell a pointer reads the current prefix, a lookup arrow jumps to a hash-map table of prefix to count and highlights the entry for current minus k, the matching subarray bracket lights on the array and the answer counter rises. A short side panel shows a sliding window on 3, 4, -3, 2, 1, 1 shrinking past a valid subarray and missing it. Actual Python code visible in readable chunks synced to the voice.
items.everyday_anchor: none: audience is working engineers; technical explanation only.
items.example: EXAMPLE nums = [3, 4, -3, 2, 1, 1], k = 3: answer 3 (subarrays [3], [4, -3, 2], [2, 1]). [1, 2, 3] k = 3 gives 2; [1, 1, 1] k = 2 gives 2; [1, -1, 0] k = 0 gives 3. Sliding window on the first array returns 1 (wrong). Brute force for n = 20000 checks 200,010,000 subarrays vs 20,000 steps (EXAMPLE).
items.code_outline: seen = {0: 1}; s = ans = 0; for x in nums: s += x; ans += seen.get(s - k, 0); seen[s] = seen.get(s, 0) + 1; return ans. Query before insert.
facts_to_verify: Problem paraphrased from the doocs mirror of LeetCode 560 (fetched): negatives allowed; prefix-sum + hash-map, seen={0:1}, query before insert, O(n) time and space. Prefix sum definition from Wikipedia.

Code run: 3, 2, 2, 3 for the four examples; 0 mismatches vs brute force on 5000 random arrays; sliding window gave 1 on [3,4,-3,2,1,1] k=3 (true 3). Sliding-window-fails-with-negatives is our own derivation. 200,010,000 vs 20,000 is EXAMPLE arithmetic.

hook_candidates.text: Majority Element सिर्फ़ दो variables से, hash map के बिना।
Majority Element problem: hash map के बिना O(1) space में कैसे?
Majority Element में hash map लगाया, interviewer बोला O(1) space!

items.one_idea: Majority Element: when a value appears more than n/2 times, keep one candidate and one counter; a different element cancels one vote, and because the majority outnumbers all other elements put together, the candidate left at the end is the majority (Boyer-Moore voting, O(n) time, O(1) space).
items.visual_idea: A row of cells for 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2 with a CANDIDATE box and a COUNT counter below; each step a ring moves over a cell and the counter ticks up or down, equal and different cells cancel in pairs with a connecting line, the candidate box swaps from 2 to 1 and back to 2 when the count hits zero, and a leftover cell stays lit as the answer. A short side panel shows the brute-force count table growing with a quadratic n by n grid. Actual Python code visible in readable chunks synced to the voice.
items.everyday_anchor: none: audience is working engineers; technical explanation only.
items.example: EXAMPLE nums = [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2], n = 7: majority is 2 (appears 4 times, more than 3). Trace (candidate, count) after each element: (2,1) (2,2) (2,1) (2,0) (1,1) (1,0) (2,1); the candidate flips to 1 at the fifth element and back to 2 at the end. [3, 2, 3] gives 3; [1] gives 1; [-1, -1, 5, -1, 7] gives -1. Brute force for n = 50000 does up to 2,500,000,000 comparisons vs 50,000 steps (EXAMPLE, the problem's upper bound for n).
items.code_outline: m = cnt = 0; for x in nums: if cnt == 0: m, cnt = x, 1 else: cnt += 1 if x == m else -1; return m. Valid only when a majority (> n/2) is guaranteed; without it the result can be any element.
facts_to_verify: Problem paraphrased from the doocs mirror of LeetCode 169 (fetched this session): majority element appears more than floor(n/2) times and is guaranteed to exist; n up to 5 x 10^4; Moore voting is O(n) time and O(1) space; one pass suffices because the majority is guaranteed, otherwise a second pass confirms the candidate. LeetCode itself returns 403.

Wikipedia (fetched): candidate m and counter c, set m = x when c = 0, equal increments, different decrements; O(n) time, O(1) extra space; without a strict majority it returns some element that is not guaranteed to be the most frequent; correctness argument that unequal pairs cancel and any other value cannot exceed half.

Code run by the planner: 2, 3, 1, -1 for the four examples; 0 mismatches against brute force and a Counter on 5000 random arrays with a forced strict majority; without a majority, [1,2,3] returns 3 and [1,2] returns 1, and on 5000 random arrays with no guarantee the returned value was not a majority in 3541 of them. Builder: run the exact on-screen code in qa/d019/run.py and show its real output.

2,500,000,000 vs 50,000 is EXAMPLE arithmetic (n = 50000, the upper bound on the problem page). The 'majority outnumbers all others combined, so the survivor is the majority' wording is a plain restatement of the Wikipedia pairing argument.
